I am 58 years old and have farmed our family's land in Quzhou for over thirty years. My husband works part-time in town now, so I make most of the day-to-day decisions on the farm. I finished middle school, so I can read the fertilizer bags and understand what the extension agent says, but honestly, I trust what I have seen with my own eyes more than anything written on paper.

This year, like every year, I will grow winter wheat and summer maize on my eight mu of land. The wheat is already in the ground from last October — I planted the improved Jimai variety that the seed station sells. It has done well for me the past few years, better than the old traditional seeds my mother-in-law used. For the summer maize, I will buy fresh hybrid seeds in June right after the wheat harvest. I never save maize seed because the hybrids lose their vigor, and I learned that lesson years ago.

For fertilizer, the extension fellow told me 15 kg of nitrogen per mu for wheat is enough, but I always put a little more to be safe — last year I held back and the wheat looked yellow at jointing. So this year I will use about 15 kg N per mu on the wheat, plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 3 kg of potassium as compound fertilizer at the base. For the maize, I will do 13 kg N, 5 kg P, and 2 kg K — the maize is hungrier at the start but the season is shorter. I split the nitrogen: half at sowing, half at the big喇叭口 stage.

I irrigate the wheat three times — once when it greens up after winter, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if the spring is dry. The maize usually gets two irrigations, one right after sowing if the soil is too dry, and one at tasseling. Pumping water costs money, so I watch the sky and talk to my neighbors; if everyone is irrigating, I irrigate too.

For tillage, I rotary-till before planting the wheat to break up the soil. But between wheat harvest and maize sowing, I have less than a week — sometimes only four or five days — so I plant the maize without tillage, just direct seeding into the stubble. Everyone in our village does it this way now; there is no time to plough.

Pesticides are necessary. For wheat, I spray four times: herbicide once in early spring, insecticide twice when the aphids come, and fungicide once at heading to prevent powdery mildew. For maize, three times is enough: herbicide at sowing, insecticide twice for the corn borer. I do the spraying myself with the backpack sprayer.

I expect about 480 kg per mu from the wheat and 520 kg per mu from the maize if the weather holds. That is what I got two years ago, and last year was a bit worse because of the dry May, so I am being cautious.

decision.reasoning_summary: I stick to the wheat-maize double cropping system because it is what our land and climate suit, and it gives my family both grain to eat and grain to sell. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because they give higher yields than traditional varieties, even though the hybrid maize seed costs money every year. I apply nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium based on what has worked before, with a little extra nitrogen as insurance because a bad yield hurts more than wasting a few yuan on fertilizer. I irrigate three times for wheat and twice for maize, which is what my neighbors do and what my experience says is enough if the year is normal. I rotary-till for wheat but plant maize without tillage because the window between wheat harvest and maize sowing is only a few days. I spray pesticides four times on wheat and three times on maize to control weeds, aphids, and disease, because if I skip a spray and the pests come, I lose too much yield.
